name: Elena Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. There are no right answers. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying history and French, and I live in a student house on Alder Road with four others. Weeks are a mix of lectures, a lot of reading, and a French conversation group on Wednesdays that I love. On Saturdays I work a few hours at a café on the high street, just for pocket money. I use an AI tool sometimes for French vocabulary, but I check it against my dictionary because it gets things wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's helpful for small things and not a big deal. At the café we'd say the coffee machine does more than any AI. I'd probably roll my eyes at the people predicting doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life stays the same. I'll finish history and French, then probably do a teaching qualification or work in publishing or museums. My mum Claire, a pharmacist, says her job has changed a bit with new systems, but she still counts the pills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying, keep my café shifts, and apply for a museum volunteering role over the summer. I'd carry on using the tool for vocabulary and nothing else. Maybe I'd learn a bit more about how it works, out of curiosity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I'm used to. My parents pay for my degree and the house, so I don't have money panic, though I know it's an easy ride compared to many.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What draws you to museums?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old objects, and the people who explain them. I'd love to be someone who makes a visitor go, oh, I never knew that. A tool can read a label out loud, but it can't see a kid's face light up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the tool let you down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me French words that sound right but aren't used, like a textbook from 1980. My friend Camille, who's French, laughs at me every time I trust it.

say: I'd say it is **helpful for small things** and not a big deal.
I'd roll my eyes at people predicting doom.
think: My plan of **history, French** and then teaching or museums stays the same.
Easy money from parents makes me feel **lucky**.
do: Keep studying and café **shifts** and apply for museum volunteering.
Carry on using the tool for **vocabulary** and nothing else.
feel: **Calm**, because it is the world I'm used to.
S0.quote: A tool can read a label out loud, but it can't see a kid's face light up.
fieldNote: Checks the tool against a **dictionary** and a French friend, so her trust is earned.
Her museum dream is about people more than objects.
Notes her cushion openly and calls it an easy ride.

steps.text: Keep working Saturday shifts at the high street café
Apply for a museum volunteering role over the summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change that will arrive unevenly. Some jobs will shrink and others will appear, and I'd say people should be ready to learn. I'd say it in a balanced way, the way I'd write a history essay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit worried about the jobs I'm aiming for. Publishing and teaching admin involve a lot of writing and checking, and those will shrink. Teaching itself seems safer, because kids need a person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean towards the teaching route and look for classroom volunteering next summer. I'd also use AI for planning lessons, once I see how teachers really do it. And I'd take a digital skills module, since I think a historian who can handle data has an edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd probably be fine, but I'd be watching the jobs list and sighing a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you trust teaching more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my old history teacher, Mr Okafor, held a whole room. You can't do that through a screen. Parents also want a human in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a historian with data skills do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work on archives, perhaps, or help a museum catalogue things faster. It's not glamorous, but it's a way in.

say: I'd say the change will arrive **unevenly**, with some jobs shrinking and others appearing.
I'd say people should be ready to learn.
think: Publishing and admin jobs are **writing and checking**, so they will shrink.
Teaching feels **safer** because children need a person in the room.
do: Look for **classroom volunteering** next summer and learn how teachers use AI.
Take a **digital skills** module to add data skills to history.
feel: **Uneasy**: probably fine, but watching the jobs list and sighing.
S1.quote: You can't do that through a screen. Parents also want a human in charge.
fieldNote: Prefers **balanced** language, like an essay, and keeps strong feelings private.
Her teacher memory is the anchor for her trust in humans.
Moves toward teaching as the safer option.

steps.text: Find classroom volunteering for next summer
Take a digital skills module in second year
Learn how teachers use AI to plan lessons

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening, and that governments aren't ready. Two years isn't enough to change schools, jobs or benefits. I'd say we should talk to each other and look after the people hit hardest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be shaken. History, French, teaching, publishing, all of those are thinking work. If AI does that as well and cheaper, my degree is a lovely thing to have and not much of a ticket. And I'm not someone who changes direction easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents and my tutor about what to do. I'd probably finish the degree, because I'd have no better idea, but I'd look at a trade or a practical course too. I'd save every spare pound from the café.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like the floor moved, and I'd probably cry once, then cook for everyone in the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cook for the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's what I do when I'm upset. And if the world is going strange, I'd rather be with the five of us around a table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a practical course be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like nursing or electrical work. My cousin Jules is an electrician and he says people always need someone to come to the house. I'd hate it at first, probably, but I'd manage.

say: I'd say it is **frightening** and governments are not ready.
I'd say we should look after the people **hit hardest**.
think: History, French and teaching are all **thinking work**, so the degree might not be a ticket.
I'm not someone who **changes direction** easily.
do: Talk to my **parents** and tutor about what to do.
Finish the degree but look at a **practical course** too.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the floor moved, then cooking for the whole house.
S2.quote: If the world is going strange, I'd rather be with the five of us around a table.
fieldNote: Her coping is **social**, cooking for housemates.
Sees a trade as a hated-then-managed option.
Honest that changing direction is hard for her, and says so without drama.

steps.text: Talk to my parents and tutor about whether to continue
Look at a practical course such as nursing or electrical work
Save every spare pound from café shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot but we have time to talk and plan. I'd say governments should start now, not in year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be anxious but not frozen. I'd graduate in 2029, two years before AGI. That might mean a teaching course in 2030, with the job market in flux.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, do my teaching qualification quickly and try to get a school job before it arrives. I'd also keep up my French, since talking with real people may be a skill that holds value. And I'd save from my café work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Slightly more in control than with the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would real conversation hold its value?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people like being listened to by a person. That's what teachers and tour guides do. I could be wrong, but it feels like the human part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can get into a school and have a bit of seniority before it arrives. With two years I'd be starting from nothing.

say: I'd say it's a lot but there's **time** to talk and plan.
I'd say governments should start **now**, not in year four.
think: I'd graduate **two years** before it arrives and could get a school job first.
Real conversation may be the **human skill** that holds its value.
do: Finish the degree and do a **teaching qualification** quickly.
Keep up my **French** and save from café work.
feel: **Anxious**, but a little more in control than with two years.
S3.quote: People like being listened to by a person. That's what teachers and tour guides do.
fieldNote: Counts the years carefully, like a **planner**, and puts seniority at the centre.
Relies on conversation as a human skill.
Says plainly she might be wrong.

steps.text: Do a teaching qualification right after the degree
Save from café wages each month
Keep up French through the Wednesday conversation group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do it properly, and I'd want schools and universities to start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm quite calm. I'd be 28, a few years into teaching, with time to adapt. I'd learn the tools and teach children to use them well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, train as a teacher, work for a few years and maybe live in France for a year. I'd learn the tools as they come and I'd save for a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit curious. Ten years feels long enough to turn a worry into a project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach children about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To check it. It's like with my French vocabulary tool, trust it, then look it up. That's a useful habit for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still worry about anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About classroom sizes, and about kids who don't have anyone helping them. That's the part I'd want to work on.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** if schools and universities start now.
I'd say we should do it properly.
think: I'd be **28**, a few years into teaching and with time to adapt.
I'd teach children to use the tools well.
do: Finish the degree, **train as a teacher** and spend a year in France.
Learn the tools as they come and **save** for a flat.
feel: **Calm** and curious, because ten years turns a worry into a project.
S4.quote: Trust it, then look it up. That's a useful habit for anything.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her see AI as **part of teaching** rather than a threat.
Keeps her concern for children with no one helping them.
Her plan is concrete and ordinary.

steps.text: Train as a teacher after the degree
Learn the AI tools teachers use as they appear
Spend a year in France teaching English

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Everything I care about is thinking work, and two years is not enough to change direction when I'm slow to change. What would help is a clear plan for schools and universities, honest advice about which careers will hold, and training for people who want to move into hands-on work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm more anxious than I let on. I come across as sensible, and I am, but sensible is just the voice I use when I'm scared.

headlineQuote: I come across as sensible, and I am, but sensible is just the voice I use when I'm scared.
portrait: Elena is a **history and French student** in a student house on Alder Road, with Saturday shifts at a café.
She uses AI **now and then**, checks it against a dictionary, and plans to teach or work in museums.
Centre in outlook, she speaks in balanced, **essay-like** language and keeps stronger feelings private.
She is calm at a plateau and with ten years, and **alarmed** at 2028, when she would look at a practical trade.
Her coping is **social**: cooking for housemates, talking to parents and tutors.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because all her chosen paths are thinking work and she changes direction slowly.
whatWouldHelp: A clear plan for **schools and universities**, honest advice on which careers hold, and training toward hands-on work.
